children.label: a
children.prompt: Verify whether $x=3$ is a solution to $x-3=0$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=3-3\\&=0\\\text{RHS}&=0\end{aligned}$$
LHS = RHS, so $x=3$ is a solution.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Verify whether $x=5$ is a solution to $\dfrac{7}{3}=\dfrac{2x}{3}-1$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\frac73\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{2(5)}3-1\\&=\frac{10}3-\frac33\\&=\frac73\end{aligned}$$
LHS = RHS, so $x=5$ is a solution.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Verify whether $y=4$ is a solution to $y^2=2y+12$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4^2\\&=16\\\text{RHS}&=2(4)+12\\&=20\end{aligned}$$
LHS $\ne$ RHS, so $y=4$ is not a solution.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Verify whether $y=6$ is a solution to $y^2=2y+12$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=6^2\\&=36\\\text{RHS}&=2(6)+12\\&=24\end{aligned}$$
LHS $\ne$ RHS, so $y=6$ is not a solution.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Verify whether $y=7e^{-3x}$ is a solution of $y'=-3y$.

answer.worked:
$y'=-21e^{-3x}$.

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=y'\\&=-21e^{-3x}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=-3y\\&=-3(7e^{-3x})\\&=-21e^{-3x}\end{aligned}$

LHS = RHS, so it is a solution.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Verify whether $y=4e^{2x}$ is a solution of $y'=-3y$.

answer.worked:
$y'=8e^{2x}$.

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=y'\\&=8e^{2x}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=-3y\\&=-3(4e^{2x})\\&=-12e^{2x}\end{aligned}$

LHS $\ne$ RHS, so it is not a solution.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Verify whether $y=\tan x$ is a solution of $y'=1+y^2$.

answer.worked:
$y'=\sec^2x$.

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=y'\\&=\sec^2x\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=1+y^2\\&=1+\tan^2x\\&=\sec^2x\end{aligned}$

LHS = RHS, so it is a solution on any interval where $\tan x$ is defined.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Show that $y=Ae^{-3x}$ is a solution of $y'=-3y$ for all values of $A$.

answer.worked:
$y'=-3Ae^{-3x}$.

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=y'\\&=-3Ae^{-3x}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=-3y\\&=-3(Ae^{-3x})\\&=-3Ae^{-3x}\end{aligned}$

LHS = RHS for every constant $A$, so it is a solution for all values of $A$.

content.prompt: Verify that the given function satisfies the DE for every value of the arbitrary constant $C$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=Ce^x-1\\\mathrm{RHS}&=x+y\\&=x+Ce^x-x-1\\&=Ce^x-1\\&=y'\end{aligned}$$
The DE is satisfied for every $C$.

$$\begin{aligned}y'&=Ce^{-x}-Cxe^{-x}\\&=Ce^{-x}(1-x)\\\mathrm{LHS}&=xy'\\&=Cxe^{-x}(1-x)\\\mathrm{RHS}&=y(1-x)\\&=Cxe^{-x}(1-x)\end{aligned}$$
LHS equals RHS for every $C$.

$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\cos(x+C)\\\mathrm{LHS}&=(y')^2\\&=\cos^2(x+C)\\\mathrm{RHS}&=1-y^2\\&=1-\sin^2(x+C)\\&=\cos^2(x+C)\end{aligned}$$
LHS equals RHS for every $C$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{C}{x^2}\\\mathrm{RHS}&=\frac{2-y}{x}\\&=\frac{2-\left(\frac{C}{x}+2\right)}{x}\\&=-\frac{C}{x^2}\\&=\frac{dy}{dx}\end{aligned}$$
The DE is satisfied for every $C$ on an interval where $x\ne0$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $y=e^{-x}$ and $y=e^{3x}$ are each solutions of $y''-2y'-3y=0$.

answer.worked:
For $y=e^{-x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=-e^{-x},\\y''&=e^{-x}.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=e^{-x}-2(-e^{-x})-3e^{-x}\\&=e^{-x}+2e^{-x}-3e^{-x}\\&=0=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$
For $y=e^{3x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3e^{3x},\\y''&=9e^{3x}.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=9e^{3x}-2(3e^{3x})-3e^{3x}\\&=9e^{3x}-6e^{3x}-3e^{3x}\\&=0=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $y=Ae^{-x}+Be^{3x}$ is also a solution for any constants $A$ and $B$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=-Ae^{-x}+3Be^{3x},\\y''&=Ae^{-x}+9Be^{3x}.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=y''-2y'-3y\\&=(Ae^{-x}+9Be^{3x})-2(-Ae^{-x}+3Be^{3x})-3(Ae^{-x}+Be^{3x})\\&=A(1+2-3)e^{-x}+B(9-6-3)e^{3x}\\&=0=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus it is a solution for any constants $A$ and $B$.

$$\begin{align*}y'&=\sec^2 x\\y''&=2\sec^2 x\tan x\end{align*}$$
The right-hand side is
$$\begin{align*}2yy'&=2\tan x\cdot\sec^2 x\\2yy'&=2\sec^2 x\tan x\\2yy'&=y''\end{align*}$$
Check the initial conditions:
$$\begin{align*}y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1\\y'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2\end{align*}$$
Therefore $y=\tan x$ is a solution of the IVP.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}-y^2&=0\\y&=0\end{aligned}$$
On $y=k$, $y'=-k^2$, which is constant along each horizontal line.
For every $x\ne0$, $-1/x^2<0$, so $y'$ is never zero.
On $x=k$, $y'=-1/k^2$, independent of $y$. Exclude $k=0$, where the differential equation is undefined.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right)&=0\\\frac{\pi x}{4}&=\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\\x&=2+4n\end{aligned}$$ where $n\in\mathbb Z$.
On $x=k$, $y'=\cos(\pi k/4)$, which is constant along the vertical line.
$$\begin{aligned}1-x+y&=0\\y&=x-1\end{aligned}$$

On $y=x+k$,
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=1-x+(x+k)\\y'&=1+k.\end{aligned}$$
The gradient is constant on each line.

The differential equation requires $x\ne0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\frac{y(2-x)}{x}\\y(2-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Thus the zero-slope loci are $y=0$ and $x=2$, within the domain.

answer.short: $y=0$ is also an obvious isocline; it is already included in (i).
answer.worked: On $y=0$, $y'=0$ for all $x\ne0$. This is the horizontal zero-slope isocline.

The differential equation requires $y\ne-1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\frac{x(1-y)}{y+1}\\x(1-y)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Thus the zero-slope loci are $x=0$ and $y=1$, within the domain.

Apart from $x=0$ and $y=1$, horizontal and vertical lines do not give constant gradients. Other isoclines are curved: setting the gradient to a nonzero constant $k$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{x(1-y)}{y+1}&=k\\x-xy&=ky+k\\y&=\frac{x-k}{x+k}.\end{aligned}$$
Here $x\ne-k$ and points with $y=-1$ are excluded.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why we can write $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=kV$ from this information.

answer.short: The rate $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ is proportional to the volume $V$, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=kV$ for a constant $k<0$.
answer.worked: Let $V$ be the volume of water and $t$ the elapsed time. Proportionality gives $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=kV$ for a constant $k$. Since the vessel is being emptied, $\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0$ when $V>0$, so $k<0$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $V=Ae^{kt}$ is a general solution to this differential equation.

answer.worked:
Differentiating $V=Ae^{kt}$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dV}{dt}&=kAe^{kt}\\&=kV.\end{aligned}$$
Thus $V=Ae^{kt}$ satisfies the differential equation for arbitrary constant $A$.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Initially, it has $100\text{ m}^3$ of water.

answer.short: $V=100e^{(\ln0.9)t/5}$, with $V$ in cubic metres and $t$ in minutes.
answer.worked:
Using $V=Ae^{kt}$, with $t$ in minutes:
$$\begin{aligned}100&=Ae^0\\A&=100\\90&=100e^{5k}\\e^{5k}&=0.9\\5k&=\ln0.9\\k&=\frac{\ln0.9}{5}\\V&=100e^{(\ln0.9)t/5}.\end{aligned}$$
Here $V$ is measured in cubic metres.

content.prompt:
A radioactive substance has initial mass 100 g. After 10 years, 80 g remains.
The rate of decay is proportional to the mass. Find the mass after 25 years, correct to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the mass in grams and $t$ the time in years.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dM}{dt}&=kM\\\frac{dM}{M}&=k\,dt\\\ln|M|&=kt+C\\M&=Ae^{kt}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $M(0)=100$, $A=100$.
$$\begin{aligned}80&=100e^{10k}\\k&=\frac{\ln(0.8)}{10}\\M(25)&=100e^{\frac{25\ln(0.8)}{10}}\\&=100(0.8)^{5/2}\\&\approx57.2\text{ g}.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
The number of bacteria $N$ in a culture grows at a rate proportional to $N$:
$$\frac{dN}{dt}=kN,$$
where $t$ is the time in hours and $k$ is an unknown constant. There are 600 bacteria after 1 hour and 1350 bacteria after 3 hours.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the general solution of this DE.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{dN}{N}&=k\,dt\\\ln|N|&=kt+C\\N&=Ae^{kt}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Substitute both data points into the solution, then divide one equation by the other to find $k$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}Ae^{k}&=600\qquad(1)\\Ae^{3k}&=1350\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{align*}e^{2k}&=\frac{1350}{600}\\e^{2k}&=\frac94\\2k&=\ln\frac94\\k&=\ln\frac32.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the number of bacteria after 5 hours, to the nearest whole number.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}N&=400e^{t\ln(3/2)}\\N&=400\left(\frac32\right)^t\\N(5)&=400\left(\frac32\right)^5\\&=3037.5\\&\approx3038.\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Every part is explicitly scaffolded. Part a is routine separation of variables. Part b is the hardest essential step: substitute two data points, divide the equations to eliminate A, and simplify ln(9/4)/2 to ln(3/2). The task tells the student to do this, so little independent planning is needed. Parts c and d are direct substitution and evaluation, with a simplification to (3/2)^t. This is harder than p53-q1, where k comes from a single point once A is known, because here two simultaneous exponential equations must be combined. It is easier than p54-q5, which adds a restructuring and mental-check part, and than p58-q9, where the dividing strategy is not signposted.

content.prompt:
According to Fick's law, diffusion across a cell membrane satisfies:
$$\frac{dC}{dt}=k(S-C),$$
for some constant $k$, where $C(t)$ is the concentration in the cell and $S$ is the concentration in the surrounding medium.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the general solution of this DE.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dC}{S-C}&=k\,dt\\-\ln|S-C|&=kt+C_1\\S-C&=Be^{-kt}\\C&=S-Be^{-kt}\\C&=S+Ae^{-kt},\end{align*}$$
where $A=-B$ is an arbitrary constant. The equilibrium solution $C=S$ is included when $A=0$.
$$\begin{align*}C_0&=S+Ae^0\\C_0&=S+A\\A&=C_0-S\\C&=S+(C_0-S)e^{-kt}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A radioactive material decays at a rate proportional to the amount present:
$$\frac{dR}{dt}=kR,$$
where $R$ is the amount at time $t$ days and $k$ is an unknown constant.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the general solution of this DE.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{dR}{R}&=k\,dt\\\int\frac{dR}{R}&=\int k\,dt\\\ln|R|&=kt+C\\R&=Ae^{kt}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Initially there is 100 grams. Determine the arbitrary constant.

answer.worked:
$R(0)=100$, so
$$\begin{align*}100&=Ae^0\\A&=100\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: After 4 days only 20 grams remain. Determine the value of $k$.

answer.worked:
$R(4)=20$, so
$$\begin{align*}100e^{4k}&=20\\e^{4k}&=\frac15\\4k&=\ln\left(\frac15\right)\\k&=\frac14\ln\left(\frac15\right)\\k&=-\frac14\ln5\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence determine the amount present after 12 days.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Show that $R=100\times\left(\frac15\right)^{t/4}$, then use this formula to check part d mentally.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}R&=100e^{kt}\\R&=100e^{\frac{t}{4}\ln(1/5)}\\R&=100\left(\frac15\right)^{t/4}\end{align*}$$
For $t=12$, there are three 4-day periods, so
$$\begin{align*}R(12)&=100\left(\frac15\right)^3\\R(12)&=\frac{100}{125}\\R(12)&=\frac45\text{ g}\\R(12)&=0.8\text{ g}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A metal ingot is cooled to $5^\circ\mathrm{C}$ then placed in a room at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Let $H$ be the temperature after $t$ minutes.

$$\frac{dH}{dt}=k(H-25),\quad\text{for some constant }k.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the general solution of this DE.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{dH}{H-25}&=k\,dt\\\ln|H-25|&=kt+C\\H-25&=Ae^{kt}\\H&=25+Ae^{kt}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use the initial condition to determine the arbitrary constant.

answer.worked:
Using $H(0)=5$:
$$\begin{align*}5&=25+A\\A&=-20\\H&=25-20e^{kt}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: After 10 minutes the ingot is at $15^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Determine the value of $k$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find how long it takes, to the nearest minute, for the temperature to reach $24^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}25-20e^{kt}&=24\\e^{kt}&=\frac{1}{20}\\kt&=-\ln20\\t&=\frac{-\ln20}{-\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\ln2}\\t&=\frac{10\ln20}{\ln2}\\t&\approx43\text{ minutes}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The atmospheric pressure $P$ on a planet changes with altitude $h$ at a rate proportional to $P$:
$$\frac{dP}{dh}=kP,$$
for some constant $k$. Let $P=P_0$ at ground level.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the general solution of this DE.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dP}{P}&=k\,dh\\\ln|P|&=kh+C\\P&=Ae^{kh}.\end{align*}$$
At ground level, $h=0$ and $P=P_0$, so $A=P_0$.
$$P=P_0e^{kh}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The pressure at $10\,000\text{ m}$ is $40\text{ kPa}$ (kilopascals) and at $6000\text{ m}$ is $80\text{ kPa}$. Find the value of $k$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Determine the pressure at ground level, correct to the nearest kPa.

answer.worked:
From (1):
$$\begin{align*}P_0&=80e^{-6000k}\\P_0&=80e^{6000\ln 2/4000}\\P_0&=160\sqrt2\text{ kPa}\\P_0&\approx226\text{ kPa}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Show that $y = e^x + \frac{\sin x}{2} - \frac{\cos x}{2}$ is a solution of the differential equation $y' = y + \cos x$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y'&=e^x+\frac{\cos x}{2}+\frac{\sin x}{2}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}y+\cos x&=e^x+\frac{\sin x}{2}-\frac{\cos x}{2}+\cos x\\&=e^x+\frac{\sin x}{2}+\frac{\cos x}{2}\end{align*}$$
LHS = RHS, so it is a solution.

content.prompt:
For which of the following differential equations is $y=2e^{2x}$ a solution?
(A) $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-4y=8e^{2x}$
(B) $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-4y=e^{2x}$
(C) $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-2\frac{dy}{dx}=0$
(D) $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=2e^{2x}\\y'&=4e^{2x}\\y''&=8e^{2x}\end{align*}$$
Test (C):
$$\begin{align*}y''-2y'&=8e^{2x}-2(4e^{2x})\\&=0\end{align*}$$
So $y=2e^{2x}$ satisfies (C). The answer is (C).

content.prompt: If $y=e^{2x}$ is a solution to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}-ky=5e^{2x}$, find the value of $k$.

answer.worked:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x}$$
Substitute into the differential equation:
$$\begin{align*}2e^{2x}-ke^{2x}&=5e^{2x}\\(2-k)e^{2x}&=5e^{2x}\\2-k&=5\\k&=-3\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
What are the values of $p$ for which $y=e^{px}$ satisfies the differential equation $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-\frac{dy}{dx}-12y=0?$$
(A) $p=-4,\; p=3$
(B) $p=-3,\; p=4$
(C) $p=\pm 3$
(D) $p=\pm 4$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y'&=pe^{px}\\y''&=p^2e^{px}\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the DE:
$$\begin{align*}p^2e^{px}-pe^{px}-12e^{px}&=0\\e^{px}(p^2-p-12)&=0\\(p-4)(p+3)&=0\end{align*}$$
Since $e^{px}\ne0$, $p=-3$ or $p=4$. The answer is (B).

content.prompt: Which differential equation is best represented by the slope field?

answer.worked:
At $y=0$, the slope field has vertical line elements, so $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is undefined. This rules out options B and D.
At $(x,y)=(2,1)$, the slope field has positive slope. For option A:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1-x}{y} &= \frac{1-2}{1} \\
&= -1
\end{align*}$$
For option C:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{(1-x)^2}{y} &= \frac{(1-2)^2}{1} \\
&= 1
\end{align*}$$
The equation represented by the slope field is option C.
Correct answer: C.

content.prompt:
A chemical dissolves in a pool at a rate equal to $5\%$ of the amount of undissolved chemical.
Initially the amount of undissolved chemical is $8\text{ kg}$ and after $t$ hours, $x$ kilograms has dissolved.
Which of the following differential equations would model this process?
(A) $\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{8-x}{20}$
(B) $\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{x-8}{20}$
(C) $\frac{dx}{dt}=-\frac{x}{20}$
(D) $\frac{dx}{dt}=8-\frac{x}{20}$

answer.worked:
The amount of undissolved chemical is $(8-x)$ kg, and the dissolving rate is $5\%$ of this.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dx}{dt}&=0.05(8-x)\\&=\frac{8-x}{20}\end{align*}$$
The answer is (A).

content.prompt:
It is given that
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5}{y}$$
and $y=-4$ when $x=0$.
Find $y$ as a function of $x$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\int y \, dy &= \int 5 \, dx \\
\frac{y^2}{2} &= 5x + C \\
& \quad \\
\text{When } x = 0, y = -4: \\
\frac{(-4)^2}{2} &= 0 + C \\
\frac{16}{2} &= C \\
C &= 8 \\
& \quad \\
\frac{y^2}{2} &= 5x + 8 \\
y^2 &= 10x + 16 \\
y &= \pm\sqrt{10x + 16} \\
& \quad \\
\text{Since } y = -4 \text{ when } x = 0\\
\text{we take the negative root:} \\
y &= -\sqrt{10x + 16}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Given that $y=f(x)$, what is the solution to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=5-y$, where $f(3)=4$?

$\text{A. }y=5-e^{x-3}$
$\text{B. }y=5-e^{3-x}$
$\text{C. }x=5y-\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{25}{2}$
$\text{D. }x=5y-\frac{y^2}{2}-9$

answer.worked:
Separate variables and integrate.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= 5-y \\
\frac{dy}{5-y} &= dx \\
-\ln|5-y| &= x+C \\
\ln|5-y| &= -x+C
\end{align*}$$
Hence $5-y=Ae^{-x}$, so $y=5-Ae^{-x}$.
Use $f(3)=4$.
$$\begin{align*}
4 &= 5-Ae^{-3} \\
Ae^{-3} &= 1 \\
A &= e^3
\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= 5-e^3e^{-x} \\
&= 5-e^{3-x}
\end{align*}$$
Correct answer: B.

content.prompt:
The equation $y=e^{ax}$ satisfies the differential equation $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+\frac{dy}{dx}-6y=0$.
What are the possible values of $a$?

$\text{A. }a=-2\text{ or }a=3$
$\text{B. }a=-1\text{ or }a=6$
$\text{C. }a=2\text{ or }a=-3$
$\text{D. }a=1\text{ or }a=-6$

answer.worked:
For $y=e^{ax}$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=ae^{ax}$ and $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=a^2e^{ax}$.
$$\begin{align*}
a^2e^{ax}+ae^{ax}-6e^{ax} &= 0 \\
e^{ax}(a^2+a-6) &= 0 \\
a^2+a-6 &= 0 \\
(a+3)(a-2) &= 0 \\
a &= -3,\ 2
\end{align*}$$
Correct answer: C.

content.prompt:
Find the values of $a$ and $b$ if $y=e^{-x}+ax+b$ is a solution to the differential equation
$$y'+y=x.$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= e^{-x}+ax+b \\
y' &= -e^{-x}+a
\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $y'+y=x$:
$$\begin{align*}
(-e^{-x}+a)+(e^{-x}+ax+b) &= x \\
ax+a+b &= x
\end{align*}$$
Equating coefficients:
$$\begin{align*}
a &= 1 \\
a+b &= 0 \\
b &= -1
\end{align*}$$
Therefore $a=1$ and $b=-1$.

content.prompt:
A thermometer, reading $24^\circ\text{C}$, is brought into a room whose temperature is $5^\circ\text{C}$.
At five minutes, the thermometer registers $18^\circ\text{C}$.
Assume that the temperature $T$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate proportional to the difference between the temperature on the thermometer and the temperature of the room; that is:
$$\frac{dT}{dt}=k(T-5)$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that $T=5+Ae^{kt}$ is a solution to the differential equation above.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dT}{dt}&=kAe^{kt}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}k(T-5)&=k(5+Ae^{kt}-5)\\&=kAe^{kt}\end{align*}$$
LHS = RHS, so it is a solution.

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
How long will it take for the thermometer to read $10^\circ\text{C}$?
Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
At $t=0$, $T=24$:
$$\begin{align*}24&=5+A\\A&=19\end{align*}$$
At $t=5$, $T=18$:
$$\begin{align*}18&=5+19e^{5k}\\e^{5k}&=\frac{13}{19}\\k&=\frac15\ln\left(\frac{13}{19}\right)\end{align*}$$
When $T=10$:
$$\begin{align*}5&=19e^{kt}\\e^{kt}&=\frac5{19}\\t&=\frac{5\ln\left(\frac5{19}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{13}{19}\right)}\\&\approx17.6\end{align*}$$
It will take approximately $18$ minutes.

content.prompt:
It is given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\sqrt{4-y^2}$ and $y=\sqrt{3}$ when $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$.
Find $y$ as a function of $x$.

answer.short: $y=2\sin(x+\pi/6)$ on the local branch containing $x=\pi/6$; the sine expression satisfies the original square-root DE only where $\cos(x+\pi/6)\geq0$.
answer.worked:
Separating the variables and integrating,
$$\begin{align*}
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-y^2}}\,dy &= \int dx \\
\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) &= x+C.
\end{align*}$$
Using $y=\sqrt{3}$ when $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$,
$$\begin{align*}
\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) &= \frac{\pi}{6}+C \\
\frac{\pi}{3} &= \frac{\pi}{6}+C \\
C &= \frac{\pi}{6}.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) &= x+\frac{\pi}{6} \\
\frac{y}{2} &= \sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \\
y &= 2\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right).
\end{align*}$$
For the initial sine branch, $-2\pi/3\le x\le\pi/3$ and $\cos(x+\pi/6)\ge0$, so $2\cos(x+\pi/6)=\sqrt{4-y^2}$.

content.prompt:
An egg at room temperature, $20^\circ\text{C}$, is placed in a saucepan of boiling water which is maintained at $100^\circ\text{C}$.
When the egg has been in the boiling water for $t$ minutes the internal temperature of the egg is $T^\circ\text{C}$.
The rate at which the internal temperature of the egg rises is proportional to the difference between the egg's internal temperature and that of the boiling water, so that $T$ satisfies the equation $\frac{dT}{dt}=k(T-100)$, where $k$ is a constant.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dT}{dt}&=kAe^{kt}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}k(T-100)&=k(100+Ae^{kt}-100)\\&=kAe^{kt}\end{align*}$$
LHS = RHS, so $T=100+Ae^{kt}$ satisfies the equation.

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The internal temperature of the egg rises to $60^\circ\text{C}$ after $10$ minutes.
Find the values of $A$ and $k$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: How long does it take the internal temperature of the egg to reach $90^\circ\text{C}$?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}90&=100-80e^{-\frac{t\ln2}{10}}\\e^{-\frac{t\ln2}{10}}&=\frac18\\-\frac{t\ln2}{10}&=-3\ln2\\t&=30\end{align*}$$
It takes $30$ minutes.

children.label: iv
children.prompt:
What would happen to the internal temperature of the egg if the egg was left in the water indefinitely?
Justify your answer.

answer.worked:
Since $k<0$, $e^{kt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.
$$T=100-80e^{kt}\to100$$
The temperature approaches $100^\circ\text{C}$.

content.prompt:
Liquid is poured into a large vertical circular cylinder at a constant rate of $1600\text{ cm}^3\text{s}^{-1}$.
At the same time, water is leaking from a hole in the base of the cylinder at a rate that is proportional to the square root of the height of the liquid present in the cylinder.
It is given that the area of the circular cross-section of the cylinder is $4000\text{ cm}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that at time $t$ seconds, the height $h$ cm of liquid in the cylinder satisfies the differential equation
$$\frac{dh}{dt} = 0.4 - c\sqrt{h}$$
where $c$ is a constant.

When $h = 25\text{ cm}$, water is leaking from the hole at a rate of $400\text{ cm}^3\text{s}^{-1}$.

answer.worked:
When $h = 25$, the leakage rate is $400\text{ cm}^3\text{s}^{-1}$:
$$\begin{align*}
k\sqrt{25} &= 400 \\
5k &= 400 \\
k &= 80
\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}
c &= \frac{k}{4000} \\
&= \frac{80}{4000} \\
&= 0.02
\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Show that the time taken to fill the cylinder from being empty to having a height of $100\text{ cm}$ is given by the integral:
$$\int_0^{100} \frac{50}{20 - \sqrt{h}}\,dh$$

children.label: d
children.prompt:
Using the substitution $\sqrt{h} = 20 - x$, or otherwise, evaluate the integral in part c.
Give your answer correct to the nearest second.

answer.worked:
Let $\sqrt{h} = 20 - x$. Then $h = (20 - x)^2$ and $dh = -2(20 - x)\,dx$. When $h=0$, $x=20$; when $h=100$, $x=10$.
$$\begin{align*}
\int_0^{100} \frac{50}{20 - \sqrt{h}}\,dh &= \int_{20}^{10} \frac{50}{x}\left[-2(20-x)\right]\,dx \\
&= \int_{10}^{20} \frac{100(20-x)}{x}\,dx \\
&= \int_{10}^{20} \left(\frac{2000}{x} - 100\right)\,dx \\
&= \left[2000\ln x - 100x\right]_{10}^{20} \\
&= 2000\ln 2 - 1000 \\
&\approx 386.29
\end{align*}$$
The time taken is approximately $386\text{ s}$.

content.prompt:
A model for the population, $P$, of elephants in Serengeti National Park is
$$P=\frac{21000}{7+3e^{-\frac{t}{3}}}$$
where $t$ is the time in years from today.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Show that $P$ satisfies the differential equation
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{1}{3}\left(1-\frac{P}{3000}\right)P$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dP}{dt}&=\frac{21000e^{-\frac t3}}{\left(7+3e^{-\frac t3}\right)^2}\\&=\frac{21000}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\cdot\frac{e^{-\frac t3}}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\end{align*}$$
Also
$$\begin{align*}1-\frac{P}{3000}&=1-\frac{7}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\\&=\frac{3e^{-\frac t3}}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\end{align*}$$
So
$$\begin{align*}\frac13\left(1-\frac P{3000}\right)P&=\frac13\cdot\frac{3e^{-\frac t3}}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\cdot\frac{21000}{7+3e^{-\frac t3}}\\&=\frac{dP}{dt}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: What does the model predict that the eventual population will be?

answer.worked:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-\frac t3}\to0$:
$$\begin{align*}P&\to\frac{21000}{7}\\&=3000\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: What is the annual percentage rate of growth today?

answer.worked:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dP}{dt}&=\frac13\left(1-\frac{2100}{3000}\right)2100\\&=210\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Rate}&=\frac{210}{2100}\\&=0.1\\&=10\%\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A spherical water purification tablet is added to a tank of water.
After $t$ hours, the tablet is a sphere with radius $r\text{ mm}$, surface area $A\text{ mm}^2$ and volume $V\text{ mm}^3$.
The tablet dissolves with a rate of change of volume directly proportional to its surface area, such that
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=-k_1A,$$
where $k_1$ is a positive constant.
Let $V_0$ be the volume at $t=0$.
You may assume the formulae $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and $A=4\pi r^2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Solve $\frac{dV}{dt}=-k_2V^{\frac{2}{3}}$ to obtain $V$ in terms of $t$, $k_2$ and $V_0$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dV}{dt} &= -k_2V^{\frac{2}{3}} \\
V^{-\frac{2}{3}}\,dV &= -k_2\,dt \\
\int V^{-\frac{2}{3}}\,dV &= -\int k_2\,dt \\
3V^{\frac{1}{3}} &= -k_2t+C
\end{align*}$$
At $t=0$, $V=V_0$.
$$\begin{align*}
3V_0^{\frac{1}{3}} &= C \\
3V^{\frac{1}{3}} &= -k_2t+3V_0^{\frac{1}{3}} \\
V^{\frac{1}{3}} &= V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-\frac{k_2t}{3} \\
V &= \left(V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-\frac{k_2t}{3}\right)^3
\end{align*}$$
This physical formula applies for $0\le t\le 3V_0^{1/3}/k_2$, while the tablet has nonnegative volume.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
In six hours $\frac{7}{8}$ of the volume of the tablet has dissolved.
Express $k_2$ in terms of $V_0$.

answer.worked:
If $\frac{7}{8}$ of the volume has dissolved, then $V=\frac{V_0}{8}$ when $t=6$.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{V_0}{8} &= \left(V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-\frac{k_2(6)}{3}\right)^3 \\
\frac{V_0}{8} &= \left(V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-2k_2\right)^3 \\
\frac{V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}}{2} &= V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-2k_2 \\
2k_2 &= \frac{V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}}{2} \\
k_2 &= \frac{V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}}{4}
\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: How long, to the nearest minute, does it take for $99\%$ of the volume of the tablet to dissolve?

answer.worked:
For $99\%$ dissolved, $V=\frac{V_0}{100}$. Using $k_2=\frac{V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}}{4}$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{V_0}{100} &= \left(V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}-\frac{V_0^{\frac{1}{3}}}{12}t\right)^3 \\
\frac{V_0}{100} &= V_0\left(1-\frac{t}{12}\right)^3 \\
\frac{1}{100} &= \left(1-\frac{t}{12}\right)^3 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{100}} &= 1-\frac{t}{12} \\
t &= 12\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{100}}\right)
\end{align*}$$
Thus $t\approx 9.41468$ hours, which is approximately $9$ hours and $25$ minutes.

content.prompt:
A large cylindrical water tank with a base radius of $0.4$ m has a tap at the bottom.
This tap allows water to flow out of the tank at a rate of $\frac{dV}{dt}=k\sqrt{h}$, where $V$ m$^3$ is the volume of water, $h$ is the depth of the water in metres, $t$ is the time in minutes and $k$ is a constant.
Initially, the water in the tank is $1$ m deep.
Twenty minutes after the tap has been turned on, the water in the tank is $0.36$ m deep.

answer.worked:
$V=\pi(0.4)^2h=0.16\pi h$, so $\frac{dV}{dh}=0.16\pi$ and
$$\begin{align*}k\sqrt h&=0.16\pi\frac{dh}{dt}\\\frac{dt}{dh}&=\frac{0.16\pi}{k}h^{-1/2}\\t&=\frac{0.32\pi}{k}\sqrt h+C\end{align*}$$
When $t=0$, $h=1$: $C=-\frac{0.32\pi}{k}$, so
$$t=\frac{0.32\pi}{k}\left(\sqrt h-1\right)$$
When $t=20$, $h=0.36$:
$$\begin{align*}20&=\frac{0.32\pi}{k}(0.6-1)\\20k&=-0.128\pi\\k&=-0.0064\pi\\&=-\frac{4\pi}{625}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: How long will it take for the tank to empty, correct to the nearest minute?

answer.worked:
The tank is empty when $h=0$:
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{0.32\pi}{k}(0-1)\\&=\frac{0.32\pi}{0.0064\pi}\\&=50\end{align*}$$
It takes $50$ minutes.

content.prompt:
A rectangular reservoir has a horizontal base of area $1000\text{ m}^2$.
At time $t=0$, the reservoir is empty and water begins to flow into it at a constant rate of $30\text{ m}^3\text{ s}^{-1}$.
At the same time, water begins to flow out at a rate proportional to $\sqrt{h}$, where $h\text{ m}$ is the depth of the water at time $t$ seconds.
When $h=1$, $\frac{dh}{dt}=0.02$.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Show that $h$ satisfies the differential equation:
$$\frac{dh}{dt}=0.01(3-\sqrt{h}).$$

answer.worked:
With $V=1000h$, $\frac{dV}{dt}=1000\frac{dh}{dt}=30-k\sqrt h$, so
$$\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{30-k\sqrt h}{1000}$$
When $h=1$, $\frac{dh}{dt}=0.02$:
$$\begin{align*}0.02&=\frac{30-k}{1000}\\k&=10\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dh}{dt}&=\frac{30-10\sqrt h}{1000}\\&=0.01(3-\sqrt h)\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The differential equation is transformed using the substitution $x=3-\sqrt{h}$.
Show that the resulting differential equation is:
$$(x-3)\frac{dx}{dt}=0.005x.$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}h&=(3-x)^2\\\frac{dh}{dx}&=-2(3-x)\\&=2(x-3)\end{align*}$$
Also $\frac{dh}{dt}=0.01x$. Then
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dh}{dt}&=\frac{dh}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}\\0.01x&=2(x-3)\frac{dx}{dt}\\(x-3)\frac{dx}{dt}&=0.005x\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Given that $x=3$ when $t=0$, find $t$ as a function of $x$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dt}{dx}&=\frac{x-3}{0.005x}\\&=200\left(1-\frac3x\right)\\t&=200\left(x-3\ln|x|\right)+C\end{align*}$$
When $t=0$, $x=3$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=200(3-3\ln3)+C\\C&=-200(3-3\ln3)\end{align*}$$
$$t=200\left(x-3\ln|x|-3+3\ln3\right)$$

answer.short: At either intersection, $m_1m_2=(-y/x)(x/y)=-1$, so the tangents are perpendicular.
answer.worked:
For $xy=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}x\frac{dy}{dx}+y&=0\\m_1&=-\frac{y}{x}.\end{aligned}$$

$$m_1m_2=\left(-\frac{y}{x}\right)\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=-1.$$
Therefore the tangents are perpendicular.

$$\begin{align*}0+4&=C_2\\C_2&=4\\x^2+2y^2&=4.\end{align*}$$
Differentiate implicitly:
$$\begin{align*}2x+4yy'&=0\\y'&=-\frac{x}{2y}\qquad(y\ne0).\end{align*}$$
The derivative is undefined at $(2,0)$, where the ellipse has a vertical tangent.

children.prompt: Both curves are drawn below. The tangents to the parabola and ellipse are perpendicular where they intersect. Why?

spec.description: Red parabola and blue ellipse on black axes, with unit ticks and no grid.
spec.mathematics: y=x²/2 and x²+2y²=4 intersect twice above the x-axis.
spec.answerVisibility: Both curves are permanent student givens.

answer.worked:
At either intersection, the gradients are $m_1=\dfrac{2y}{x}$ and $m_2=-\dfrac{x}{2y}$. Neither $x$ nor $y$ is zero there.
$$\begin{align*}m_1m_2&=\frac{2y}{x}\left(-\frac{x}{2y}\right)\\&=-1.\end{align*}$$
The gradients are negative reciprocals, so the tangents are perpendicular.

content.prompt:
A conical tank (height $12\text{ m}$, radius $4\text{ m}$) is filled with water that evaporates at a rate proportional to the circular surface area. Let $r$ metres be the radius of the surface at time $t$ hours.

(Volume of cone: $V=\frac13\pi r^2h$.)

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down a DE for the evaporation in terms of the radius.

answer.worked:
The circular surface area is $\pi r^2$. Since evaporation decreases the volume,
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=k\pi r^2,\qquad k<0.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use part a and the chain rule to find a DE for the rate of change of the radius.

answer.worked:
By similar triangles, $\dfrac{h}{r}=\dfrac{12}{4}=3$, so $h=3r$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac13\pi r^2h\\V&=\pi r^3\\\frac{dV}{dt}&=3\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}.\end{align*}$$
Using part a, while $r>0$,
$$\begin{align*}3\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}&=k\pi r^2\\\frac{dr}{dt}&=\frac{k}{3}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use the given information to solve this DE.

answer.worked:
Separate variables and integrate:
$$\begin{align*}dr&=\frac{k}{3}\,dt\\\int dr&=\int\frac{k}{3}\,dt\\r&=\frac{k}{3}t+C.\end{align*}$$
Initially the tank is full, so $r=4$ when $t=0$. Thus $C=4$ and
$$r=\frac{k}{3}t+4.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: After $6$ hours the depth of water is $10.5\text{ m}$. Determine the value of $k$.

answer.worked:
At $t=6$, $h=10.5$, so $r=\dfrac{10.5}{3}=3.5\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}3.5&=\frac{k}{3}(6)+4\\2k&=-0.5\\k&=-\frac14.\end{align*}$$
Hence $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=-\dfrac1{12}\text{ m/h}$ and $r=4-\dfrac{t}{12}$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Hence give a formula for the volume of water at time $t$. Note any restrictions on $t$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^3\\V&=\pi\left(4-\frac{t}{12}\right)^3.\end{align*}$$
The model applies from the initial full tank until it is empty. Setting $r=0$ gives $4-\dfrac{t}{12}=0$, so $t=48$ hours. Thus $0\le t\le48$, with $V$ in cubic metres.

content.prompt: Find $y=f(x)$ given $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{2y+6}$, the function passes through $(1,0)$ and the function is:

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dx}{dy}&=2y+6\\x&=\int(2y+6)\,dy\\x&=y^2+6y+C\end{align*}$$
At $(1,0)$:
$$\begin{align*}1&=0+0+C\\C&=1\\x&=y^2+6y+1\\y^2+6y+(1-x)&=0\\y&=\frac{-6\pm\sqrt{36-4(1-x)}}{2}\\y&=-3\pm\sqrt{x+8}\end{align*}$$
For an increasing function, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}>0$, so $y>-3$. Therefore
$$y=-3+\sqrt{x+8},\qquad x>-8.$$
This branch satisfies $y(1)=0$.

answer.short: No solution satisfies all the stated conditions.
answer.worked:
At the given point $(1,0)$,
$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,0)}=\frac{1}{2(0)+6}=\frac16>0.$$
Thus a solution through $(1,0)$ cannot be decreasing. The decreasing branch of $x=y^2+6y+1$ is $y=-3-\sqrt{x+8}$, but it gives $y(1)=-6$, so it does not satisfy the initial condition.

content.prompt:
A cylindrical tank is filled with water to a height of 400 cm. A tap at the bottom is opened and
$$\frac{dh}{dt}=k\sqrt{h}.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: State the initial condition, and explain why $k$ must be negative.

answer.worked: $h(0)=400$. While there is water in the tank, $\sqrt{h}>0$ and $\dfrac{dh}{dt}<0$. Therefore $k<0$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Solve the IVP. You may assume the arbitrary constant of integration is positive.

answer.worked:
Separate variables:
$$h^{-1/2}\,dh=k\,dt.$$
Integrating gives
$$2\sqrt{h}=kt+C.$$
At $t=0$, $h=400$, so
$$\begin{aligned}C&=2\sqrt{400}\\C&=40.\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{h}&=kt+40\\h&=\left(\frac{kt+40}{2}\right)^2\\h&=\frac14(kt+40)^2.\end{aligned}$$
The unsquared equation requires $kt+40\geq0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: After 20 minutes the height is 100 cm. Find two possible values of $k$.

answer.short: The squared expression gives the candidates $k=-1$ and $k=-3$.
answer.worked:
Using $h(20)=100$ in the squared expression:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac14(20k+40)^2&=100\\(20k+40)^2&=400\\20k+40&=\pm20\\k&=-1\text{ or }-3.\end{aligned}$$
These are algebraic candidates; their validity in the draining model is checked in part d.

children.label: d
children.prompt: How long does the tank take to drain? Hence explain why only one value of $k$ is valid.

answer.short: 40 minutes. The candidate $k=-3$ gives an empty tank after $\dfrac{40}{3}$ minutes, before the stated observation at 20 minutes. Only $k=-1$ is valid.
answer.worked:
For $k=-1$, set $h=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac14(-t+40)^2&=0\\t&=40\text{ min}.\end{aligned}$$
For $k=-3$, set $h=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac14(-3t+40)^2&=0\\t&=\frac{40}{3}\text{ min}.\end{aligned}$$
But there is still water in the tank after 20 minutes. The candidate $k=-3$ would empty the tank before then; extending its squared expression would incorrectly make the water level rise again. Therefore only $k=-1$ is valid, and the tank drains after 40 minutes.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Is the function found in part b valid for larger values of $t$?

answer.short: No. The draining formula is valid for $0\leq t\leq40$ minutes. The tank remains empty afterwards.
answer.worked: No. With $k=-1$, the formula is $h=\dfrac14(40-t)^2$. For $t>40$, this expression increases again, implying that the water level rises after the tank has emptied. It also violates $2\sqrt{h}=40-t$. Thus the draining formula is valid only for $0\leq t\leq40$ minutes; afterwards $h=0$.

entries.description: Solving dy/dx = f(x)

The simplest type of differential equation is \(\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)\).
To solve these equations, integrate both sides with respect to \(x\).
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}&=f(x)\\\int\frac{dy}{dx}\,dx&=\int f(x)\,dx\\y&=\int f(x)\,dx\\&=F(x)+C\end{aligned}\]
The general solution of a DE contains constant \(C\) and represents a whole family of curves.
Remember that your solution is an equation; you must have \(y=\cdots\).

entries.description:
An application of differential equations you have seen before is exponential growth and decay.
For exponential change, the rate of change is directly proportional to the current amount.
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.
Growth constant: k positive for growth; k negative for decay.
If Q = Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt} = kQ.
A is labelled “initial quantity”, “t = 0”; k in the exponent is identified by an arrow from the growth-constant annotation.
k gives the growth rate, A is the initial condition.

emphasis: directly proportional to the current amount
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.

entries.description:
In realistic models of growth and decay, the change is proportional to the difference of the current value to some constant value, P.
Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.
If Q = P + Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt}
= k(P + Ae^{kt} − P)
= k(Q − P).
An underbrace beneath P + A labels it “initial quantity”, “t = 0”.
The left graph is labelled k < 0, A > 0. The right graph is labelled k < 0, A < 0.
When k < 0 (decreasing growth), the quantity Q approaches a limiting value P as t → ∞.
This limiting value P can represent:
• ambient temperature; hot objects cool towards room temperature.
• carrying capacity; populations stabilise at the maximum an environment can support.
P is a horizontal isocline of the slope field, representing the constant asymptotic solution.

emphasis: Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.

entries.description:
dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C)

The logistic equation models growth that is limited by a carrying capacity C.
kP represents exponential growth, and (1 − P/C) represents the constraints of the environment.
When P = C, (1 − P/C) = 0 and growth stops.

Logistic growth in a population begins slowly as few individuals reproduce, accelerates as the population grows, then slows as it approaches the environment's carrying capacity.

[Paired graphs]

The logistic equation has horizontal isoclines representing constant asymptotic solutions at P = 0 and P = C. All solution curves will tend to converge towards P = C.
Usually, the scenario limits the domain and range to t ≥ 0 and P > 0.

Alternate notation:
P′ = kP(C − P): C is expanded into the brackets; k is different to the original.

entries.description:
The general form of a logistic differential equation dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C) is

P = C/(1 + Ae^(−kt)) where A = (C − P₀)/P₀.

Note that you cannot memorise this. The questions will require you to solve the DE.
To solve the DE, you will be given a partial fraction decomposition and follow these steps:

1. Invert both sides of the DE to get dt/dP.
2. Match the integrand to the given partial fractions.
3. Integrate both sides; use D as the constant of integration.
4. Combine ln a − ln b = ln(a/b) and isolate.
5. Exponentiate and write ±e^(c/k) as a single arbitrary constant A.
6. Substitute the initial condition to find A.
7. Rearrange to make P the subject.
8. Divide through by e^(kt) to reach the general form P = C/(1 + Be^(−kt)).

We will first practice the purely algebraic case where there is no context.

entries.description:
A colony of rabbits has carrying capacity 1200 and satisfies
\[\frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{1200}\right),\qquad P(0)=200,\quad P(2)=400,\]
where k is an unknown constant and t is in years.
Use \(\frac{1200}{P(1200-P)}=\frac1P+\frac1{1200-P}\).
Find P(t) and hence P(5).
entries.presentation: Black question text; centred differential equation and initial conditions. Unbordered working space below. The supplied decomposition establishes the separation-of-variables and partial-fractions method.

entries.description:
Supplied blue working:
\[\frac{dt}{dP}=\frac1k\left(\frac1P+\frac1{1200-P}\right)\Rightarrow\frac{P}{1200-P}=Ae^{kt}.\]
\[P(0)=200:\quad\frac{200}{1000}=A\Rightarrow A=\frac15,\text{ so }P=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-kt}}.\]
Find k using P(2)=400:
\[400=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-2k}}\Rightarrow1+5e^{-2k}=3\Rightarrow e^{-2k}=0.4.\]
\[k=-\frac12\ln0.4=\frac12\ln2.5\approx0.4581.\]
\[P(5)=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-5k}},\text{ where }e^{-5k}=(0.4)^{2.5}\approx0.1012.\]
\[P(5)=\frac{1200}{1.5060}\approx797.\]

entries.description: Solve the differential equation to find the formula for the height of the tree.

Separate variables:
[1/(Q(45 − Q))] dQ = 0.03 dt
Using partial fractions from (a):
(1/45)(1/Q + 1/(45 − Q)) dQ = 0.03 dt
Integrate both sides:
(1/45)(ln|Q| − ln|45 − Q|) = 0.03t + C
ln|Q/(45 − Q)| = 1.35t + C
Q/(45 − Q) = Ae^(1.35t)
Sub initial condition Q = 0.3 when t = 0:
0.3/44.7 = A → A = 1/149
So: Q/(45 − Q) = (1/149)e^(1.35t)
149Q = (45 − Q)e^(1.35t)
149Q + Qe^(1.35t) = 45e^(1.35t)
Q(149 + e^(1.35t)) = 45e^(1.35t)
Q = 45e^(1.35t)/(149 + e^(1.35t))
Divide numerator and denominator by e^(1.35t):
Q = 45/(1 + 149e^(−1.35t))

entries.description:
A lake is stocked with 600 fish; the carrying capacity is 12 000. The population N satisfies
\[\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(12\,000-N),\]
with t in years. You may use
\[\frac{12\,000}{N(12\,000-N)}=\frac1N+\frac1{12\,000-N}.\]
entries.presentation: Opening text followed by a centred differential equation, then the time-unit statement and supplied partial-fraction identity. Three parts follow in order.
Provide working space for the derivation.

entries.description: The population doubled during the first year. Find k.
Find, to the nearest month, how long it takes the population to reach 9000.

Supplied blue solution:
“The alternate notation gives the scaling”
\[\frac{dt}{dN}=\frac1{12\,000k}\left(\frac1N+\frac1{12\,000-N}\right),\]
“so the exponent is 12 000kt.”
\[\frac{N}{12\,000-N}=Ae^{12\,000kt};\qquad N(0)=600:\quad\frac{600}{11\,400}=A=\frac1{19}\]
\[19N=(12\,000-N)e^{12\,000kt}\]
\[N=\frac{12\,000}{1+19e^{-12\,000kt}}\]
entries.presentation: Blue answer-only content, positioned on the right below the question; retain equation order and alignment.
Blue answer-only content; successive displayed equations.

entries.description:
Supplied blue solution:
“Set N = 9000:”
\[1+19e^{-12\,000kt}=\frac{12\,000}{9000}=\frac43\]
\[e^{-12\,000kt}=\frac1{57}\]
\[12\,000kt=\ln57\]
“Since \(12\,000k=\ln\dfrac{19}{9}\):”
\[t=\frac{\ln57}{\ln(19/9)}\approx5.411\text{ years}\approx65\text{ months}\]
entries.presentation: Blue answer-only content; preserve the exact expression and supplied intermediate approximation.

entries.description:
Kosciusko National Park has feral horses called brumbies.
Brumbies are considered pests as they damage the soil and waterways.
Their natural population P satisfies dP/dt = 0.5P(1 − P/20 000), with t in years.
To control it, a culling programme aims to remove 10% of the population each year, giving
 dP/dt = 0.5P(1 − P/20 000) − 0.1P
Populations above 15 000 damage the habitat.
Determine whether the culling programme would be effective in preventing this damage.
entries.presentation: Black question text; natural-population equation inline and culling-model equation centred on a separate line. Unruled working space below. No parts, diagrams or tables.

entries.description: Supplied blue worked answer, separate from the student prompt.
entries.expectedAnswer:
Find the non-zero equilibrium (where dP/dt = 0):
P[0.5(1 − P/20 000) − 0.1] = 0
For P ≠ 0:
0.5(1 − P/20 000) = 0.1
1 − P/20 000 = 0.2
P = 16 000
The population settles at 16 000.
Since 16 000 > 15 000, the culling programme is not ambitious enough to prevent damage to the habitat.

entries.description:
An application of differential equations you have seen before is exponential growth and decay.
For exponential change, the rate of change is directly proportional to the current amount.
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.
Growth constant: k positive for growth; k negative for decay.
If Q = Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt} = kQ.
A is labelled “initial quantity”, “t = 0”; k in the exponent is identified by an arrow from the growth-constant annotation.
k gives the growth rate, A is the initial condition.
entries.mappingNote: The same independently inventoried source teaching passage continues in this separately authored native wrapper. Source text and original inventory entry retained; current independent content review covers this exact wrapper.

entries.description:
In realistic models of growth and decay, the change is proportional to the difference of the current value to some constant value, P.
Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.
If Q = P + Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt}
= k(P + Ae^{kt} − P)
= k(Q − P).
An underbrace beneath P + A labels it “initial quantity”, “t = 0”.
The left graph is labelled k < 0, A > 0. The right graph is labelled k < 0, A < 0.
When k < 0 (decreasing growth), the quantity Q approaches a limiting value P as t → ∞.
This limiting value P can represent:
• ambient temperature; hot objects cool towards room temperature.
• carrying capacity; populations stabilise at the maximum an environment can support.
P is a horizontal isocline of the slope field, representing the constant asymptotic solution.

entries.description:
dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C)

The logistic equation models growth that is limited by a carrying capacity C.
kP represents exponential growth, and (1 − P/C) represents the constraints of the environment.
When P = C, (1 − P/C) = 0 and growth stops.

Logistic growth in a population begins slowly as few individuals reproduce, accelerates as the population grows, then slows as it approaches the environment's carrying capacity.

[Paired graphs]

The logistic equation has horizontal isoclines representing constant asymptotic solutions at P = 0 and P = C. All solution curves will tend to converge towards P = C.
Usually, the scenario limits the domain and range to t ≥ 0 and P > 0.

Alternate notation:
P′ = kP(C − P): C is expanded into the brackets; k is different to the original.
